families.name: Bantu
families.description: Largest language family in Kenya (~65% of population). Spread across central, western, and coastal regions.

families.name: Nilotic
families.description: Second largest family (~30%). Includes Plains Nilotes (Maasai, Turkana, Samburu, Teso), Highland Nilotes (Kalenjin, Pokot), and River-Lake Nilotes (Luo).

families.name: Cushitic
families.description: Found in northern and eastern Kenya (~3%). Includes Somali, Borana/Oromo, Rendille, and Daasanach (Dhaasanac).

families.name: Other
families.description: Includes Swahili (Bantu-based national & official lingua franca), English (official), and minor language isolates.

languages.name: Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ)
languages.notes: Largest mother-tongue community in the central highlands; documented in Höhnel (1894), Hémery (1903), Hinde (1904), McGregor (1904), Routledge (1910), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Dholuo (Luo)
languages.notes: River-Lake Nilotes of the Lake Victoria basin; documented in Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902), Northcote (1907), Roscoe/Willis (1915), Mill-Hill Fathers (1920), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Kalenjin
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Nandi, Kipsigis, Tugen, Marakwet, Keiyo, Sabaot); documented in Hollis (1909), Dundas (1910), BFBS (1921), Diercks & Rao (2019), Landman (2019), and Zwarts, Chelimo & Jerono (2024).

languages.name: Luhya (Luyia)
languages.notes: 17+ Western Bantu dialects including Wanga, Bukusu/Masaba, and Maragoli (Logoori); documented in Hobley (1902, 1903), Purvis (1909), Roscoe (1915), Johnston (1919), Stam (1929), and Payne, Pacchiarotti & Bosire eds. (2016).

languages.name: Kamba (Kĩkamba)
languages.notes: Central Bantu language of Eastern Kenya; documented in Krapf (1850), Last (1885), Hinde (1904), Hobley (1910), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), Lindblom (1920), BFBS (1921), and Jones & Freyer (2019).

languages.name: Somali
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language of North Eastern Kenya; documented in Cust (1883), de Larajasse (1897), Kirk (1903, 1905), BFBS (1921), Nilsson (2016), Kimper et al. (2019), and Nurse (2019).

languages.name: Kisii (Ekegusii)
languages.notes: Eastern Lake Victoria Bantu language of the Kisii Highlands; documented in Hobley (1902) and Johnston (1902, 1919).

languages.name: Meru (Kĩmĩĩrũ)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya & Tana valley Bantu cluster (Imenti, Tigania, Igembe, Mwimbi, Chuka, and Kĩtharaka); documented in Hobley (1910), Champion (1912), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and Kithaka wa Mberia (2004).

languages.name: Maasai (Maa)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Eastern Nilotic); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Cust (1883), Höhnel (1894), Hinde (1901), Hollis (1905), Hobley (1910), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Turkana (Ng'aturukana)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Ateker branch) across Turkana County; documented in Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), and Barton (1921).

languages.name: Embu (Kĩembu)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya southeastern slopes (Embu & Mbeere); documented in Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and Hobley (1922).

languages.name: Taita (Kidawida)
languages.notes: Taita Hills Bantu (Dawida, Sagala, Kasigau); documented in Shaw (1885), Taylor (1891), Wray (1894), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Swahili (Kiswahili)
languages.notes: National & official language of Kenya (including Kiamu, Kimvita, Kitikuu/Bajuni, Kipate, Kingozi, and Kiunguja); documented in Krapf (1850, 1882), Steere (1870, 1894, 1918), Taylor (1891), Bateman (1901), Madan (1903, 1917), Burt (1910), Stigand (1915), Beech (1918), Werner (1918, 1919, 1933), Mwamzandi (2022), and Goldsmith & Mpiranya (2022).

languages.name: Mijikenda
languages.notes: Nine coastal Sabaki sub-groups (Giriama, Digo, Duruma, Chonyi, Jibana, Kambe, Ribe, Rabai, Kauma); documented in Krapf (1850), Krapf & Rebmann (1887), Taylor (1891), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Nicolle (2016).

languages.name: Borana (Oromo)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language (Borana, Gabbra, Sakuye, and Tana River Orma/Bararetta); documented in Krapf (1840, 1842, 1850), Tutschek (1844–1845), Cust (1883), Foot (1913), Werner (1915), BFBS (1921), and Griefenow-Mewis (1996).

languages.name: Rendille
languages.notes: Omo-Tana East Cushitic camel-herding pastoralists of the Kaisut and Chalbi plains; documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Hobley (1910), Fleming (1964), and Heine (1976).

languages.name: Teso (Ateso)
languages.notes: Eastern Nilotic (Ateker) language spoken in Busia County and eastern Uganda; documented in Hobley (1902), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Kitching (1915), Roscoe (1915), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Pokomo
languages.notes: Tana River Sabaki Bantu language across 13 Upper and Lower Pokomo vyeti; documented in Krapf (1850), Würtz (1895), Werner (1913, 1915, 1933), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Mikael Samson & Darroch (1944).

languages.name: Samburu
languages.notes: Northern Maa (Plains Nilotic) pastoralists; documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), and Hobley (1910).

languages.name: Ilchamus (Njemps)
languages.notes: Lake Baringo Maa-speaking irrigation farmers and fishermen (En-jemusi); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Dundas (1910), and Beech (1911).

languages.name: Pokot (Pökoot)
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Northern Kalenjin branch, historically Suk); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Johnston (1902), Dundas (1910, 1915), Beech (1911), and Barton (1921).

languages.name: Taveta (Kitaveta)
languages.notes: Northeast Coast Bantu (Pare-Taveta group) around Taveta and Lake Jipe; documented in Höhnel (1894), Steggall (1892–1906), Hollis (1910–1911), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Daasanach (Dhaasanac)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic (Western Omo-Tana) agropastoral and fishing community around Ileret on the northeastern shore of Lake Turkana; documented in Höhnel (1894 as Reshiat), Sasse (1974, 1976), Tosco (2001), Nishiguchi (2004), and Blažek (2011).

officialLanguages.use: Government, judiciary, higher education, formal business
Everyday communication, National Assembly, primary education, media

notes: Kenya has 42+ recognized ethnic groups speaking 60+ distinct languages and dialects.
Speaker numbers are estimates based on KNBS 2019 Census ethnic population data (language ≈ ethnicity for most groups).
County-level language dominance is approximate. Urban areas (especially Nairobi, Mombasa) are highly multilingual.

Several Kenyan languages are classified as endangered by UNESCO, including El Molo (~300 speakers), Yaaku, Dahalo (with dental clicks, documented in Werner 1915 and Sands & Güldemann 2019), Suba, Ilchamus, and Omotik.
Data compiled from KNBS 2019 Census, UNESCO Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger, and 65 historical & contemporary linguistic works (1840–2024).
source: Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 Population and Housing Census & Constitution of Kenya
